input: The aim of this worked example is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min, using the measured rate constant k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, which was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is fixed by the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a given time is given by exp(-k t), where the rate constant and the time are the quantities that enter. Substituting the measured rate constant into these relations gives a half-life of 30.1 min and a fraction remaining of 0.25 at the stated time. It is worth noting that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and the same numerical procedure would not apply. The example is a useful illustration of the way in which, for a reaction of this kind, a single measured constant determines the whole course of the decay, since once the constant is known, the fraction remaining at any time can in principle be obtained from the same pair of relations without further measurement. As a broad internal check, the stated time is close to two half-lives, and the fraction remaining is correspondingly close to one quarter, which is consistent with the computed values.
target: Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. The rate constant k is 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is fixed by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t is exp(-k t). Substitution of the rate constant gives a half-life of 30.1 min. The fraction remaining at the stated time is 0.25. The check is internal: the stated time is close to two half-lives, and one quarter of the material remains, which matches the computed fraction. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither relation carries over to that case. The two relations are used in sequence: the rate constant first fixes the half-life, and the half-life then gives a direct reading of the fraction at any stated time, because each successive half-life halves what remains. The measurement pattern behind the rate constant matters to the result: readings spread over the full run show whether the decay stays first-order throughout, and a drift in the fitted constant would show in the later readings before it showed in the half-life. The result is therefore a statement about first-order decay at the measured rate constant: a half-life of the stated length, and a quarter of the material remaining after the stated time.
